ru: С за́втрашнего дня я бу́ду приноси́ть обе́д.
en_alt: From tomorrow I will be bringing lunch.
note: Compound future is correctly progressive; the possessive 'my' is added, so the bare-object reading is offered as an alternative.
Frame collision with the perfective is harmless: the partner is a bare imperative, which no learner would confuse with a habitual present.

ru: Он приноси́л бы газе́ту, е́сли бы вспомина́л.
note: Imperfective habitual 'would bring ... if he remembered' is correct; the partner has a present-tense coordinate clause («но магази́н закры́т») which fixes it as a present counterfactual, so neither side should move.

en_alt: The adopted law came into force.
note: The relative clause is a fair rendering of the participle; the participial alternative is added for the word-bank drill.

en_alt: I will have a shower before bed.
note: «приня́ть душ» is a fixed collocation; the British 'have a shower' is equally valid.

en_alt: He took an important decision.
note: 'take a decision' is the standard British variant of «приня́ть реше́ние».

ru: Я приняла́ бы предложе́ние без коле́баний.
Е́сли бы мог, я приобрёл бы э́ту карти́ну.
en_alt: If I could, I would acquire this painting.
note: The Russian fronts the protasis; that order is equally natural in English.

ru: Она́ бы присе́ла, но нет свобо́дных мест.
note: The present-tense coordinate clause fixes this as a present counterfactual, so plain 'would sit down' is right despite the perfective.

ru: Я сейча́с прися́ду отдохну́ть на мину́тку.
en_alt: I will sit down now to rest for a minute.
note: Trailing 'now' reads as though it modifies 'minute'; the alternative puts «сейча́с» where the Russian has it.

ru: Он бы присла́л отве́т, е́сли бы успе́л.
en_alt: He would have sent a reply if he had had time.
note: Perfective with a perfective protasis also supports the past-counterfactual reading; no partner collision forces a change to en_gb.

ru: Му́дрый руководи́тель прислу́шивался бы к лю́дям.

en_alt: They listen attentively to the opinion of the people.
note: 'heed' is a good idiomatic rendering; the literal one matching the headword gloss is added alongside.

ru: Тепе́рь я бу́ду прислу́шиваться к сове́там.
en: From now on I will listen attentively to advice.
note: 'listen to advice attentively' strands the adverb; English puts it next to the verb.

en_alt: Do you listen attentively to your father's advice?
note: 'closely' is fine; the gloss-matching 'attentively' should also be accepted.

ru: На всех испы́таниях бу́дет прису́тствовать врач.
en_alt: A doctor will be present at all the tests.
note: «всех» is 'all'; 'every' is an equally natural rendering, so both should be accepted.

ru: Я прису́тствовал бы, е́сли бы меня́ пригласи́ли.
Он приходи́л бы ча́ще, е́сли бы жил бли́же.
note: 'would come more often' is the correct habitual imperfective; the collision should be resolved on the perfective side («Он бы пришёл, е́сли бы его́ позва́ли» wants 'would have come ... had been invited'), which lives in another packet.

ru: С понеде́льника я бу́ду приходи́ть ра́ньше.
Мне ча́сто прихо́дится рабо́тать по ноча́м.

en: He had to walk a lot.
note: 'walk ... on foot' is redundant in English; 'walk' already carries «ходи́ть пешко́м».

ru: Он уме́ет пришива́ть запла́ты на брю́ки.
en_alt: He knows how to sew patches onto trousers.
note: «уме́ет» is 'knows how to'; 'can' is idiomatic but the literal reading should also be accepted.

ru: Я пришью́ наши́вку к фо́рме за́втра.
Е́сли бы нашёл и́голку, я приши́л бы пу́говицу.
en_alt: If I found a needle, I would sew on the button.
I would have sewn on the button if I had found a needle.
note: The Russian fronts the protasis, and the perfective also supports the past-counterfactual reading; both alternatives added.

en_alt: Will you sew a button onto the coat?
note: The Russian has no possessive, so the definite-article reading should also be accepted.

en_alt: I will sew a button onto the coat.
note: The Russian has no possessive, so the definite-article reading should also be accepted.

ru: Она́ приши́ла но́вый воротни́к к пла́тью.
Я пробегу́ э́тот путь за час.
Е́сли бы не уста́л, я про́бовал бы ещё раз.
note: Imperfective present counterfactual is correct; the collision comes from the perfective partner «Ты бы попро́бовала э́то блю́до», which is a protasis-less advisory and should read 'You should try this dish' — that fix belongs to попробовать's packet.

en: We have tried this soup before.
note: The past perfect implies a further past reference point the Russian never sets; the imperfective with «ра́ньше» is an experiential present perfect.

ru: За у́жином го́сти бу́дут про́бовать блю́да из ра́зных стран.
en: Over dinner, the guests will be trying dishes from different countries.
note: The imperfective compound future бу́дут + infinitive is 'will be trying', not a bare 'will try'; this one flattened future was colliding with three separate попробовать sentences at once.

en_alt: Are you trying a new dish?
note: The gloss covers both 'try' and 'taste'; both should be accepted here.

en_alt: I am trying a new dish.
note: The gloss covers both 'try' and 'taste'; both should be accepted here.

The perfective correctly reads as a single completed event; the collision is caused by the imperfective partner «бу́ду бормота́ть», which should read 'will be muttering' — that fix belongs to бормотать's packet.
Same collision source as above: the imperfective compound future partner is the half that needs 'will be muttering'.

ru: Он сейча́с пробормо́чет что́-то и уйдёт.
en: In a moment he will mutter something and leave.
note: Trailing 'now' attaches to 'leave' and misreads «сейча́с», which with a perfective future means 'in a moment'.

ru: Она́ бы пробормота́ла извине́ние и ушла́.
en_alt: She would have muttered an apology and left.
note: The remainder of the sentence already distinguishes it from the imperfective partner, so en_gb stands; the perfective past-counterfactual reading is added as an alternative.

ru: Я прове́рила бы счёт ещё раз.
en: I would have checked the bill once more.
note: Collides with the imperfective «Я проверя́л бы рабо́ту тща́тельнее» ('I would check…') in an almost identical first-person frame; forcing the perfective to a single completed event leaves 'would check' to the imperfective alone.
Frame-only collision: a bare imperative is unmistakable against the imperfective declaratives it matches on, so the drill remains answerable.

ru: С за́втрашнего дня я бу́ду проверя́ть по́чту у́тром.

note: Collides only in frame with a bare imperative, which is easy to tell apart.
This imperfective side is the correct 'would check'; the perfective partner is the half being retranslated to 'would have checked'.
The English is right — «провести́ о́пыт» is 'conduct an experiment' — but the headword gloss 'to spend' does not cover this sense; the gloss is probably the half to fix.

en_alt: Will you conduct an important experiment?
note: Same sentence pattern as its sibling but rendered 'carry out' rather than 'conduct'; both should be accepted, and the headword gloss 'to spend' still needs widening.

ru: Мы бы провели́ о́тпуск в гора́х.

en_alt: Will you accompany the guests to the door?
note: 'see … to the door' is idiomatic; the gloss-matching 'accompany' should also be accepted.

ru: По́сле ка́ждой встре́чи я бу́ду проводи́ть госте́й до вы́хода.
note: «бу́ду» + infinitive needs an imperfective, but проводи́ть in the 'see off' sense is perfective (impf. провожа́ть); as written the compound future can only be the homonymous 'spend/conduct' verb, which does not fit «госте́й до вы́хода» — needs either «бу́ду провожа́ть» or a perfective «провожу́».

The English is correct, but this is the homonymous imperfective проводи́ть 'to spend (time)', a sense the headword gloss 'to accompany' does not cover — the entry or the example needs a human decision.

ru: Я проводи́л бы тебя́, е́сли бы не спеши́л.

note: Stress: the genitive of дверь is две́ри, so «до две́ри» — as spelt correctly in this entry's own first example; «двери́» here marks the locative form.
«до до́ма» here means home, not a particular building; 'to the house' would be «к до́му».

ru: Ка́ждое у́тро она́ бу́дет провожа́ть сы́на до шко́лы.

en_alt: Are you seeing your friend off?
note: Both particle placements are equally natural English and should both be accepted.

en_alt: We are seeing the guest to the car.
We are accompanying the guest to the car.
note: The simple present reads as a habit; the progressive renderings match how the entry's other present-tense examples are translated.

en: Are you seeing your friends off to the station?
note: «на вокза́л» is accusative — motion to the station, not «на вокза́ле» 'at the station'; the case is exactly what these examples teach.

en: I am seeing my friends off to the station.
note: «на вокза́л» is accusative — motion to the station; 'at the station' would need «на вокза́ле».

ru: Она́ провожа́ла бы нас, но занята́.
Она́ проговори́ла всю ночь с подру́гой.
note: The English is right — this is the delimitative про- 'to talk for the whole night' — but the headword gloss 'to utter' does not cover it; the gloss is likely the half to widen.

ru: Он сейча́с проговори́т па́ру слов и замолчи́т.
en: In a moment he will utter a couple of words and fall silent.
note: «сейча́с» is dropped entirely from the English.

en_alt: I will utter this phrase slowly.
note: 'say' is fine, but the gloss-matching 'utter' used by the sibling examples should also be accepted.

ru: Я продава́л бы деше́вле, е́сли бы спрос был ме́ньше.
en_alt: I would sell more cheaply if demand were lower.
note: Imperfective present counterfactual is correct; the standard adverbial form is added as an alternative.
Frame-only collision against an infinitive complement ('wants to sell'); the two remain easy to tell apart.

ru: Ле́том я бу́ду продава́ть я́годы на ры́нке.

en_alt: They were selling vegetables at the market.
note: The imperfective past supports both the habitual and the progressive reading.

en_alt: Tickets are sold at the ticket office.
note: Russian has no article, and «ка́сса» is 'ticket office' as readily as 'box office'.

en_alt: The flat is sold.
note: The short passive participle supports both the stative and the present-perfect rendering.

en: He would have sold the house for more.
note: Perfective бы + past with no protasis reads most naturally as a missed opportunity; this also clears the 'would sell' collision with the imperfective «Я продава́л бы деше́вле…», which is a genuine present counterfactual.

en_alt: I am continuing to learn Russian.
note: The imperfective present supports both the simple and the progressive rendering.

ru: На сле́дующей неде́ле мы бу́дем продолжа́ть рабо́ту над прое́ктом.
en: Next week we will be continuing work on the project.
note: The imperfective compound future бу́дем + infinitive is 'will be continuing', not a bare 'will continue'; this one flattened future was colliding with three separate продо́лжить sentences at once, and «рабо́ту над прое́ктом» is a noun object, not 'working on'.

ru: Е́сли бы бы́ло вре́мя, я продолжа́ла бы учи́ться.
en_alt: If I had time, I would continue studying.
note: The Russian fronts the protasis; the imperfective 'would continue' is correct, and the collision is fixed on the perfective side.

en: He went on working all night.
note: Collides exactly in frame with the perfective «Она́ продо́лжила чита́ть кни́гу» ('She continued reading…'); the durative imperfective with «всю ночь» is better served by 'went on', which leaves plain 'continued' to the perfective.

en_alt: The meeting continued for a long time.
note: 'went on' is idiomatic; the gloss-matching 'continued' should also be accepted.

en_alt: The rain has already been going on for an hour.
note: «уже́» is unrendered in en_gb; the alternative restores it and reads more naturally.
'will be continuing all night' is not natural English here, and «всю ночь» already carries the duration; no collision forces a change.

ru: Она́ бы продо́лжила расска́з, но усну́ла.
en: She would have continued the story, but she fell asleep.
note: «но усну́ла» is a past coordinate clause, so this is a past counterfactual, not a present one; the fix also clears the 'would continue' collision with the imperfective «я продолжа́ла бы учи́ться».
The perfective future is correctly a bare 'will continue'; the collision is cleared on the imperfective compound-future side.
Plain 'continued' is right for the perfective single act; the imperfective partner is the half being moved to 'went on working'.
Correct bare future for the perfective; the collision is cleared on the imperfective compound-future side.
Correct bare future for the perfective; the collision is cleared on the imperfective compound-future side.
